vignette:
Maria's Story

Maria sits in the chair with her hands folded in her lap, her posture careful and composed-the same way she's learned to move through the world for the past six years. At seventy-four, she carries herself with the practiced grace of someone who has spent fifty years filling prescriptions, listening to patients, and maintaining the kind of professional demeanor that inspires trust. But there's a brittleness underneath now, a tension in her shoulders that never quite releases.

The incident happened in the spring of 2018, when Maria was sixty-eight. She had been married to Roberto for forty-two years, and while their relationship had grown distant over time, she hadn't imagined it could turn violent. That evening, she mentioned-carefully, she thought-that she'd been offered a part-time consulting position at a local hospital. She was excited about it, about staying engaged in her field. Roberto had been drinking. He said she was trying to make him look bad, that she thought she was better than him. When she tried to leave the room, he grabbed her arm and threw her against the kitchen counter. She fell, striking her ribs and her head. He left the house. She called their daughter, who drove her to the emergency room.

The physical injuries healed. Fractured ribs, a concussion, deep bruising. But Maria never returned to the pharmacy after that week. She told her colleagues she was retiring early. The truth was more complicated-she couldn't concentrate on the medications anymore, couldn't trust her own attention. She'd find herself staring at a prescription bottle, unable to remember what she was doing. More frighteningly, she'd become hypervigilant about errors, convinced she might poison someone. After fifty years of confidence in her work, she abandoned it entirely.

Roberto moved to his brother's house for three months, then came home with apologies and promises. Maria let him stay. She tells herself she was being practical-they were married, they had a life together-but she knows now it was something else. A kind of paralysis. She couldn't leave him, but she couldn't feel safe with him either.

The nightmares started almost immediately after the assault and haven't stopped. She wakes most nights around three in the morning, her heart racing, her sheets soaked with sweat. Sometimes she dreams she's back in the kitchen. Other times she's trapped in a small space, unable to move. She wakes gasping, and Roberto is there beside her in the darkness-sometimes asleep, sometimes awake and pretending to be. Either way, the fear doesn't distinguish.

During the day, she's learned to function through a kind of emotional numbness. She goes to church on Sundays. She cooks. She maintains her home. But she doesn't invite her daughter over anymore-the shame is too heavy. She doesn't sleep well. She startles at sudden noises, at Roberto's raised voice, at the way a door closes too quickly. Loud sounds send her back to that moment in the kitchen, and it takes her several minutes to return to the present.

She's stopped driving at night. She avoids the neighborhood where the pharmacy was. She doesn't watch the news anymore-any story about violence triggers the intrusive images. She's withdrawn from her book club, from her friends. The isolation feels safer than the risk of being known.

What troubles her most, she says quietly, is that she's still here. Still in this house with him. Still afraid. And she doesn't know how to leave.
